g.text: A quick-lookup handbook and reference guide for MRI physics formulas, sequence characteristics, tissue relaxation properties, and scanner safety
Search reference entries (e.g. T1, FLAIR, SAR, Chemical Shift)...
. A short TR does not give tissues time to fully
recover their longitudinal magnetization along the main magnetic field. Consequently, tissues with short
T1 relaxation times (such as fat) recover more longitudinal signal and appear bright, while tissues with
long T1 (such as water and CSF) stay dark. The short TE keeps transverse T2 differences from
Figure 1: Axial T1 brain scan demonstrating dark ventricular fluid and bright white matter.
Short TR (300–600 ms) and Short TE (10–25 ms).
Fat is bright, white matter is bright, gray matter is intermediate, CSF/fluid is dark.
Excellent for anatomical detail and post-contrast gadolinium studies.
Why is fluid bright on a T2-weighted image?
. The long TE allows transverse magnetization to
dephase and decay before the echo signal is acquired. Tissues with long T2 relaxation times (such as
water, CSF, and edematous fluid) retain their transverse coherence and remain bright, whereas short-
T2 tissues decay quickly and appear dark.
Figure 2: Axial T2 brain scan showing hyperintense (bright white) cerebrospinal fluid.
Long TR (> 2000 ms) and Long TE (> 80 ms).
Fluid and CSF are very bright; muscle and cortical bone are dark.
Sensitive for detecting pathology, inflammation, edema, and tumors.
How does Spin Echo differ from Gradient Echo?
uses an initial 90° RF excitation pulse followed by a 180° RF refocusing pulse. The
180° pulse inverts the dephasing spins, cancelling out fixed static field inhomogeneities and chemical
shifts to yield true T2 contrast.
refocuses transverse magnetization using a bipolar gradient reversal rather than
an RF pulse. It typically employs flip angles less than 90°, allowing much shorter TRs and faster scan
times, but remains subject to T2* susceptibility dephasing.
Figure 3: Spin echo contrast spectrum across differing TR and TE values.
Clean true T2 contrast, higher RF energy deposition (higher SAR), longer scan times.
Fast 2D/3D imaging, low SAR, sensitive to hemorrhage and iron deposits (T2*).
What is FLAIR and when is it used?
is an inversion recovery sequence designed to
suppress the high signal of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) while maintaining heavy T2 weighting in brain
tissue. By setting the Inversion Time (TI) to match the zero-crossing null point of CSF (approx. 2000–
2500 ms), fluid appears dark, making hyperintense periventricular lesions stand out clearly.
Figure 4: FLAIR brain scan with fluid nulled dark, highlighting periventricular white matter lesions.
Brain parenchyma displays T2 contrast, but ventricles and sulcal CSF are completely dark.
Standard of care for diagnosing multiple sclerosis plaques, infarction, and subarachnoid
Chemical shift artifact occurs because hydrogen protons in fat molecules precess at a slightly lower
resonant frequency than protons in water molecules (approximately 3.5 parts-per-million difference).
When frequency encoding is used to map spatial position, fat tissue is mapped a few pixels away from
its true physical location relative to water.
Figure 5: Chemical shift artifact visible at tissue boundaries along the frequency readout axis.
A dark boundary on one side of an organ and a bright boundary on the opposite side.
Occurs strictly along the Frequency-Encoding axis (never along phase encoding).
Increase receiver bandwidth (Hz/pixel) or apply fat saturation techniques.
How does Patient Motion cause Ghosting Artifacts?
Patient motion (gross head movement, eye blinking, arterial pulsation, or respiration) causes phase
errors between phase-encoding steps. Because phase encoding occurs over several seconds or
minutes across TR intervals, movement gets Fourier transformed into periodic ghost copies along the
Figure 6: Motion ghosting repeating periodically along the phase-encoding direction.
Almost always manifests along the Phase-Encoding axis.
Swap phase and frequency axes, use respiratory/cardiac gating, or use radial k-space trajectories
